question: Can a nonlinear network preserve continual trainability by placing paired sine and cosine features in every hidden layer so that some locally linear path remains available at every pre-activation?

key_findings.claim: The paper establishes only conditional trainability results for linear and diagonal deep-linear models, not a general guarantee for deep Fourier networks.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 bounds taskwise suboptimality for bounded, strongly convex linear objectives after enough gradient steps. Theorem 2 keeps the product matrix nonsingular for randomly initialized diagonal deep-linear networks under gradient descent. The Fourier-network result is instead a Taylor approximation and embedding argument.

key_findings.claim: Deep Fourier features pair sine and cosine at every layer to offer a locally near-linear unit for each pre-activation while retaining nonlinear representational paths.
key_findings.evidence: For every phase, at least one member of the sine/cosine pair lies away from a critical point and is approximated by a first-order Taylor term. The induction argument then treats the near-linear and remaining nonlinear units as jointly embedding a deep-linear subnetwork that uses all parameters.

key_findings.claim: High unit-sign entropy is a useful diagnostic but is not sufficient for plasticity.
key_findings.evidence: Linear units retain balanced signs, whereas saturating or one-sided activations lose sign diversity. Pure sine activations retain high sign entropy yet still lose trainability; the authors use that counterexample to motivate combining phase diversity with local linearity.

anchors.section: 4.1 Adding Linearity to Nonlinear Activation Functions

key_findings.claim: On the reported continual-vision tasks, deep Fourier ResNet-18 models are consistently competitive and often strongest, especially on tiny-ImageNet, but the paper does not provide exact table values or matched compute.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 5 and 6 show gains under diminishing label noise and class-incremental learning against ReLU, spectral regularization, CReLU, ReDO, shrink-and-perturb, and S-EWC. Curves and captions, rather than numerical tables, carry the main comparisons; Fourier pairing halves effective width but activation cost and tuning cost are not normalized.

key_findings.claim: Trainability and generalization separate sharply: unregularized Fourier models can overfit, while their retained gradient response permits stronger regularization and then better test performance.
key_findings.evidence: The regularization sweep shows high training accuracy but poor test accuracy for weakly regularized deep Fourier networks; at stronger spectral regularization, the Fourier models remain trainable while ReLU baselines collapse, producing the best test curves in the shown ranges.

key_findings.claim: The visual evidence supports sustained adaptation but leaves stability, forgetting, and calibration underdetermined in this preprint revision.
key_findings.evidence: The inspected plots report current-task accuracy, clean-test accuracy, and average end-of-task accuracy with ten-seed standard-error bands. They do not provide per-task forgetting matrices, backward transfer, calibration, or paired statistical tests, so plasticity cannot be read as complete continual-learning quality.

method.core_idea: Replace each hidden activation with a width-adjusted concatenation of sine and cosine so every phase has a locally linear carrier while the overall network stays nonlinear.
method.mechanism: The paper first contrasts taskwise optimization in linear, deep-linear, and nonlinear networks. It defines unit-sign entropy, tests fixed mixtures between identity and nonlinear activations, and derives a bounded local-linear approximation for paired sine/cosine units. ResNet-18 and MLP experiments then compare deep Fourier layers with common activations and plasticity interventions across changing labels, pixels, and class pools.
assumptions: Taskwise linear objectives are strongly convex or effectively bounded away from degeneracy during finite training.
Random initialization prevents two factors of a diagonal deep-linear mode from reaching zero together.
A pointwise Taylor approximation and embedded linear path translate into usable optimizer-level plasticity.
The selected nonstationarities and image benchmarks represent the plasticity failures relevant to broader continual learning.
Spectral regularization can be tuned comparably across activation families.

techniques.role: Concatenates sine and cosine after every affine map to couple phase-complete local linearity with nonlinear features.
Measures whether hidden-unit signs remain diverse across inputs rather than saturating or linearizing one-sidedly.
Interpolates an activation with the identity to diagnose how explicit linearity changes continual trainability.
Repeatedly changes labels, pixels, noise levels, or class availability and measures current-task learning over time.
Uses the Fourier network's retained trainability to tolerate stronger regularization and improve generalization.

evaluations.setting: Repeated random-label tasks on MNIST-family datasets with MLPs.
evaluations.result: Deep-linear models retain trainability; deep Fourier networks learn nonlinear random-label problems faster and remain near full training accuracy across the shown sequence.
evaluations.baseline: Identity, ReLU, sine, CReLU, shallow Fourier features, and alpha-linearized activations.

evaluations.setting: Diminishing label noise on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and tiny-ImageNet using ResNet-18.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy on the uncorrupted test set over ten tasks.
evaluations.result: Deep Fourier features finish among the best methods on all three and show their clearest visual margin on tiny-ImageNet.
evaluations.baseline: ReLU, L2 variants, spectral regularization, CReLU, ReDO, shrink-and-perturb, and streaming EWC.

evaluations.metric: Whole-test-set accuracy as five classes are added per task.
evaluations.result: Deep Fourier features substantially lead most baselines on tiny-ImageNet and remain in the top group on CIFAR-100.

evaluations.setting: Regularization, width, depth, and normalization sensitivity studies.
evaluations.metric: Training and test accuracy or average end-of-task accuracy.
evaluations.result: Fourier models scale especially well with width and remain trainable under strong regularization; extra depth helps more modestly.
evaluations.baseline: Matched ReLU MLPs, layer normalization, linearized layer normalization, and L2-to-initialization.

limitations: Author-stated through the sensitivity discussion: deep Fourier features tend to overfit without sufficient regularization.
Reviewer inference: the strongest theorem covers diagonal deep-linear networks, not the proposed nonlinear architecture or stochastic Adam training.
Reviewer inference: the Taylor remainder is local and pointwise; it does not show that optimization selects, preserves, or composes the implied linear carrier globally.
Reviewer inference: results concentrate on supervised vision and synthetic label/pixel shifts, with no language-model or reinforcement-learning evaluation in this revision.
Reviewer inference: main figures omit exact result tables, paired tests, wall-clock cost, activation throughput, and tuning-budget accounting.
Reviewer inference: current-task trainability is emphasized more than retention, backward transfer, and total continual-learning utility.
failure_modes: The paired periodic features fit label noise readily and generalize worse when regularization is too weak.
Large or poorly scaled pre-activations create rapidly oscillating features and unstable frequency sensitivity.
Strong regularization needed for generalization erases the trainability advantage on a new data or optimizer regime.
A distribution shift changes useful phases faster than gradient descent can preserve the locally linear carriers.
The doubled activation representation raises memory or kernel cost despite width matching by parameter count.
Good current-task accuracy masks catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks.
reusable_insights: Plasticity diagnostics should separate gradient responsiveness, current-task fitting, retention, and generalization.
A counterexample with high sign entropy but poor plasticity shows why single hidden-state statistics require a causal ablation.
Complementary activation pairs can guarantee local coverage of a desired derivative regime even when either member alone cannot.
Architectures that preserve trainability may create value mainly by expanding the safe regularization range, not by improving unregularized performance.
Mechanistic architecture claims should be stress-tested under matched parameters, FLOPs, wall-clock, and hyperparameter-search budgets.
open_questions: Can one prove a taskwise convergence or gradient lower bound for deep Fourier networks rather than for an embedded diagonal linear surrogate?
Does the method retain its advantage in transformers, recurrent networks, large-scale language modeling, and continual reinforcement learning?
Which regularizer is actually necessary: spectral control, weight decay, phase control, or frequency-adaptive normalization?
How do deep Fourier features trade current-task plasticity against forgetting on strict online class-incremental protocols?
Do the 2025 adaptive-linearity and activation-design methods dominate Fourier pairing under matched compute and tuning?
Can learned wavelet or frequency mixtures preserve phase coverage without the periodic model's overfitting tendency?

competitive_landscape.title: Preserving Plasticity in Continual Learning with Adaptive Linearity Injection
competitive_landscape.difference: AdaLin learns neuron-level gates that inject linearity into ReLU, Tanh, or GeLU from gradient flow, whereas deep Fourier features hard-code sine/cosine pairs and rely on phase-complete local linearity.

competitive_landscape.title: Activation Function Design Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Smooth-Leaky and Randomized Smooth-Leaky target negative-branch shape and saturation with simple drop-in nonlinearities and add nonstationary MuJoCo tests; the reviewed paper uses periodic pairs and focuses on supervised vision.

competitive_landscape.title: Sustaining Plasticity via Learnable Wavelet Activations in Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: The wavelet method learns separated low/high-frequency components, dynamically injects capacity, and regularizes old knowledge; deep Fourier features use fixed sinusoids and external regularization.

competitive_landscape.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Lyle et al. isolate several causes of plasticity loss and emphasize normalization and optimization diagnostics; the reviewed paper proposes a specific activation architecture motivated by linearity and sign entropy.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Continually by Spectral Regularization
competitive_landscape.difference: Spectral regularization directly controls weight singular values to preserve trainability and is used with deep Fourier features in the strongest generalization experiments, so some observed benefit belongs to the combination rather than the activation alone.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Deep Fourier features dynamically balance the trainability of linear models with nonlinear representational power and provide a broadly effective continual-learning activation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines conditional linear-model theory, a sine/cosine Taylor-coverage argument, unit-sign diagnostics, and supervised continual-learning experiments across three major vision datasets.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The fixed phase-paired activation and its adaptive-linearity framing were distinctive at submission and the empirical breadth is meaningful. The theorem does not establish plasticity of the proposed network, and later AdaLin, Smooth-Leaky, and wavelet activations make activation design itself a competitive family. The defensible novelty is the particular sine/cosine construction plus its diagnostic case study, not a general proof that embedded linearity solves continual learning.

reviewer_notes: Read all 22 extracted pages, including proofs, empirical appendix, references, and every displayed figure. Visually inspected the construction and principal trainability/generalization plots; axes and captions support the qualitative claims but do not expose exact tables. The PDF and arXiv record expose no first-party code repository, so no code audit was possible. Current direct competitors were checked at primary arXiv and OpenReview records on 2026-08-23.
